12900:
Proportion is about relationship — specifically, how one thing compares to another in terms of size, quantity, or importance. It answers the question: How much of one thing is there relative to something else?

Think of a pizza. If you cut it into 8 slices and you eat 2, your proportion of the pizza is 2 out of 8. The word is always pointing at a relationship, not a standalone number or thing.
Meaning 1: A Part or Share of a Whole

This is the most everyday use. When something large (a group, a quantity, a total) is divided or distributed, the share that one part makes up is called a proportion.

Examples:

  • "A large proportion of the country's population lives in cities." — Out of all the people in the country, a big share of them live in cities.
  • "Only a small proportion of applicants were accepted." — Out of all who applied, only a few made it.

Notice that proportion says something about how much of the whole a part represents. It's more meaningful than just saying "a few" or "many" — it implies a comparison to the total.
Meaning 2: The Ratio or Relationship Between Two or More Things

Proportion also describes how two (or more) things relate to each other in size or quantity — like a recipe or a formula.

Examples:

  • "The proportion of water to rice is 2 to 1." — For every 1 cup of rice, you use 2 cups of water. The relationship between the two is fixed.
  • "The proportion of men to women on the team was roughly equal."

This use is close to the word ratio. In fact, proportion and ratio are closely related. A proportion is essentially a ratio expressed in context, often with the idea that it should stay the same or is being compared to something. (In mathematics, a proportion is specifically a statement that two ratios are equal — e.g., 1:2 = 3:6. This is why we say things like "solve for x in this proportion.")
Meaning 3: Balance, Harmony, and Correct Fit Between Parts

This is a more artistic and visual meaning. When the different parts of something are the right size relative to each other, we say they are in proportion, or that the thing has good proportion.

Examples:

  • "The architect designed the building with perfect proportion — the windows, columns, and doors all looked exactly the right size relative to each other."
  • "The painter struggled to draw the human body in proportion — the head kept coming out too large for the body."

This meaning is very common in art, design, architecture, and even talking about the human face or body. A face is considered proportionate when the eyes, nose, mouth, and forehead all sit in a balanced relationship to each other — none too big, none too small.

The underlying idea is the same: each part must relate correctly to the others.
Meaning 4: Proportions (Plural) — Size, Scale, or Extent

When used in the plural form — proportions — the word shifts slightly to describe the overall size, scale, or dimensions of something, often to emphasize how large or serious it is.

Examples:

  • "The flood was a disaster of enormous proportions." — The disaster was on a huge scale.
  • "They built a hall of grand proportions." — The hall was impressively large.
  • "The problem grew to alarming proportions." — The problem became very serious and large.

Here, "proportions" is really describing magnitude — how big, how serious, how vast something is. You'll often see dramatic or emphatic language used alongside it.

These phrases use the word in a natural, everyday way and are extremely common in English.

In proportion — correctly sized or balanced relative to something else.
"Her reaction was in proportion to the situation — calm and measured."

Out of proportion — too big, too small, or too extreme relative to what is appropriate.
"His anger was completely out of proportion to what actually happened."
"In the drawing, her arms look out of proportion with her body."

A sense of proportion — the ability to judge what is more or less important; not overreacting or exaggerating.
"Keep a sense of proportion — this is a minor problem, not a catastrophe."
This is a very important idiomatic use. When someone tells you to "keep things in proportion" or that you have "lost your sense of proportion," they mean you are treating something small as though it were huge, or something minor as though it were a crisis.

Every meaning of proportion revolves around the same central idea: how one thing stands in relation to another. Whether you are talking about a share of a whole, a ratio between quantities, the balance between artistic elements, the scale of a crisis, or someone's emotional response to an event — proportion is always asking: Does the size, amount, or weight of this thing fit correctly with what it is being compared to?

When things are in proportion, they fit. When they are out of proportion, something is too much or too little relative to what it should be. That simple push and pull is the soul of this word.
12901:
When two things are proportional, it means they are related to each other in a consistent, balanced way — so that when one changes, the other changes in a matching, predictable manner, keeping the same ratio between them.

Think of it like a recipe. If a cookie recipe calls for 2 cups of flour and 1 cup of sugar, the ratio is 2:1. If you want to make double the cookies, you use 4 cups of flour and 2 cups of sugar. The amounts changed, but the relationship between them stayed the same. That is proportionality — the flour and sugar are proportional to each other.
Breaking It Down With a Simple Image

Imagine a shadow. The taller a person is, the longer their shadow. A person who is twice as tall will have a shadow that is roughly twice as long. The height and the shadow length move together in a consistent ratio. They are proportional.

Now flip it: if someone is only half as tall, the shadow is roughly half as long. It doesn't matter whether the person is short or tall — the ratio between height and shadow length stays constant. That locked-in, unchanging ratio is exactly what makes two things proportional.

A ratio is just a comparison of two quantities — like 1:2, or 3:6, or 50:100. Notice that 1:2, 3:6, and 50:100 are all actually the same ratio (they all simplify to 1:2). When two quantities are proportional, their ratio always stays the same, no matter how large or small the actual numbers get.

This is the razor-sharp definition: two quantities are proportional if their ratio remains constant.

This is a very important distinction. Proportional does not mean "the same amount." It means "the same relationship."

A small pizza might have 6 slices and a large pizza might have 12 slices. They are not equal in size. But if the small pizza costs $6 and the large one costs $12, the price is proportional to the number of slices — you're paying $1 per slice in both cases. The amounts are different, but the relationship is identical.

Since you want to know everything about this word, you need to know about two major types of proportional relationships:

Directly proportional means that as one thing goes up, the other goes up too — in the same ratio. This is what most people mean when they simply say "proportional." More hours worked → more money earned (at the same hourly rate). More fuel in the tank → more miles you can drive.

Inversely proportional means that as one thing goes up, the other goes down — but still in a consistent, predictable ratio. More workers on a job → fewer days needed to finish it. Higher speed → less time to reach your destination. The word "inversely" signals that the relationship runs in opposite directions. You will often see this written as "inversely proportional to" rather than just "proportional to."

When you see "proportional" alone, without "inversely," it nearly always means directly proportional.
How It's Used Outside of Math

"Proportional" is not just a math word. It appears widely in everyday language, and the meaning is always rooted in that same core idea — a fitting, balanced relationship between two things.

In law and justice: A punishment is said to be proportional when it fits the seriousness of the crime. A $5 fine for forgetting to return a library book is proportional. Sending someone to prison for the same offense would not be — it would be wildly out of proportion.

In everyday reactions: If a friend makes a small, accidental mistake and you respond by screaming and ending the friendship, your reaction is not proportional to what happened. A proportional response would be calm and measured — matched in scale to the size of the offense.

In art and design: A painting, a building, or a human face is said to have proportional features when each part is sized in a balanced way relative to the whole. A face where the nose is five times larger than the eyes would look strange because the proportions are off.

In politics: "Proportional representation" is a system where the number of seats a political party receives in parliament matches (is proportional to) the share of votes that party received from the public. If a party gets 30% of the votes, they get roughly 30% of the seats.

In physics and science: Scientists use "proportional" constantly. The force of gravity you feel is proportional to your mass. The brightness of a light source decreases in a way that is proportional to the square of your distance from it.

Understanding a word's opposite sharpens your understanding of the word itself. When something is out of proportion, it means the balance or ratio has been broken — one thing is too large, too small, too intense, or too extreme relative to the other.

"She blew the whole argument out of proportion" means she treated a small issue as if it were a massive one — the size of her reaction didn't match the size of the actual problem.

"The building's windows are out of proportion with its walls" means the windows are too large or too small relative to the overall structure — the ratio is off.

So "proportional" is the state of that ratio being right and consistent, while "out of proportion" is the state of that ratio being broken or distorted.
How to Use It in Sentences

• "The amount of effort you put in is usually proportional to the results you get out."
  • "The doctor said the dosage should be proportional to the patient's body weight."
  • "In a fair tax system, what you pay should be proportional to what you earn."
  • "The company's growth has been directly proportional to its investment in customer service."
  • "His anger was completely disproportional to the situation." (Note: disproportional is simply the negative form — meaning not proportional.)

If you had to boil it all down to a single sentence: something is proportional when it stays in the same consistent ratio to something else — matched in scale, balanced in relationship, and predictable in how it changes.

Everything else — the math, the law, the art, the everyday speech — is just that one idea applied to different areas of life.
12902:
Proportionate means correctly matched in size, degree, or amount relative to something else. The key phrase here is "relative to something else" — this word is never used in isolation. Something can only be proportionate to something. It always describes a relationship between two or more things.

Think of it this way: if you pour a small cup of coffee, adding one teaspoon of sugar might be proportionate. But if you make a giant pot of coffee and still add just one teaspoon of sugar, that's not proportionate — it's too little for the size of the pot. The sugar needs to match the coffee in the right ratio.

1. The Quantitative Sense (about measurable things)

This is the mathematical idea. Two things are proportionate when they increase or decrease at the same rate or ratio.

Imagine you're paid by the hour. If you work 2 hours, you earn £20. If you work 4 hours, you earn £40. If you work 6 hours, you earn £60. Your pay is proportionate to your hours — as one goes up, the other goes up by the exact same ratio. Double the hours, double the pay. The two things move in step with each other.

This is sometimes called being directly proportionate — both things move in the same direction by the same ratio.

Now here's the flip side: things can also be inversely proportionate. This means as one thing goes up, the other goes down — again, at a matching rate. For example, the more workers you hire to build a wall, the less time it takes to finish. The number of workers and the time taken are inversely proportionate. One rises as the other falls, in a corresponding, matched way.

2. The Evaluative Sense (about what is appropriate or fair)

This is the more everyday, human sense of the word — and it's used constantly in law, ethics, and daily conversation. Here, proportionate means appropriate in scale, fitting, or reasonable given the circumstances.

Imagine someone bumps into you lightly by accident. If you respond by shouting at them for an hour, your reaction is not proportionate — it is far too large a response for such a small incident. But if you simply say "watch out" or say nothing at all, that would be proportionate — your response matches the scale of what happened.

This sense of the word is essentially asking: Does the size of the response, punishment, or action correctly match the size of the situation that caused it? If yes — it's proportionate. If not — it's disproportionate.

Both senses share the same underlying logic: things are in the right, correct, or appropriate ratio to each other. Whether you're talking about numbers and measurements, or about human responses and decisions, the word always points to a kind of balance — not too much, not too little, but just right in relation to something else.

You will often see the word proportional used as well. In most everyday situations, these two words mean the same thing and can be swapped freely. However, there is a subtle difference worth knowing:

  • Proportional leans more toward the strict mathematical sense — the ratio is exactly, measurably equal.
  • Proportionate leans more toward the evaluative sense — appropriately matched, which allows for some judgment about what "correct" looks like.

So a scientist might say two variables are "proportional." A judge, a politician, or an everyday person is more likely to say a response should be "proportionate." But again — in most uses, they overlap almost entirely.

To truly understand a word, you must know its opposite. Disproportionate means the relationship is unbalanced or mismatched — one side is too large or too small relative to the other.

A disproportionate amount of blame placed on one person means that person received far more blame than their actual role in a situation deserved. A punishment that is disproportionate to the crime is either far too harsh or far too lenient. Whenever you see "disproportionate," something is out of balance — the ratio is wrong.

• Science: "The size of the dose should be proportionate to the patient's body weight." — a heavier person may need more medicine in the correct ratio.
  • Law: "The use of force must be proportionate to the threat faced." — you cannot use enormous force to respond to a tiny threat.
  • Economics: "A proportionate increase in costs led to a proportionate rise in prices." — costs and prices rose by the same ratio.
  • Everyday life: "Her grief seemed proportionate to the loss she had suffered." — her sadness made sense given how serious the loss was; it wasn't overdone or underdone.
  • Government: "The tax burden should be proportionate to income." — those who earn more should pay more, in a correctly matched ratio.

Proportionate describes something that is correctly and fittingly matched in size, degree, or amount to something else. It captures the idea of balance and right ratio — whether in numbers, where two quantities rise and fall in step with each other, or in human judgment, where a response, punishment, or action is appropriate and fair given what it is responding to. When something is proportionate, nothing is out of balance. When it is not, we call it disproportionate.
12903:
A proposal is a suggestion, plan, or offer that someone presents to others for their consideration — meaning, the other person or group gets to think about it, discuss it, and then either accept it, reject it, or modify it.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is that a proposal is not a decision. It is an invitation to make a decision. It sits at the "beginning" stage — before anything is agreed upon or set in motion.

Think of it this way: when you have an idea, a plan, or an offer in your mind, and you take that idea and formally put it in front of someone else for them to respond to — that act, and the thing you present, is called a proposal.

The moment you say, "Here is my idea. What do you think? Do you agree?" — you have made a proposal.
The Two Essential Parts of Every Proposal

Every proposal, in any situation, has two key ingredients:

1. Content — what is being suggested. This could be a plan, an idea, a request, or an offer.

2. An audience — someone who receives it and must respond. A proposal always goes from one party to another. You cannot make a proposal to yourself.

The word "proposal" appears in many different areas of life, but the core meaning stays the same in all of them. Here are the main contexts:

1. A Marriage Proposal

This is probably the most widely known use. When someone asks another person to marry them, that act is called a marriage proposal (often just "a proposal"). The person gets down on one knee, presents a ring, and says, "Will you marry me?"

Notice the structure: one person puts forward an offer, and the other person must respond — yes or no. This perfectly matches the core meaning of the word.

2. A Business Proposal

In the professional world, a proposal is a formal document or presentation in which one party (a company or individual) offers to do something for another party — often in exchange for money or a partnership.

For example, a marketing agency might send a proposal to a company saying, "Here's our plan to grow your brand. Here's what we'll do, here's the timeline, and here's the cost." The company then decides whether to accept or decline.

3. A Research or Academic Proposal

In universities and academic settings, a student or researcher writes a research proposal to describe a study they want to carry out — before actually doing it. They present the topic, the purpose, the method, and the expected results. A committee then decides whether to approve it and, often, whether to fund it.

4. A Policy or Government Proposal

In governments and organizations, a proposal is a suggested law, rule, or policy that is put forward for debate and voting. For example, "The government has put forward a proposal to reduce carbon emissions by 40% by 2035." It's not a law yet — it's a proposal. It still needs to be debated and voted on.

5. An Everyday Proposal

In less formal situations, "proposal" can simply mean any suggestion put forward for group consideration. For example: "She made a proposal that the team work four days a week instead of five." This is less formal, but the same logic applies — she suggested it, and others need to agree or disagree.

Understanding what comes before and after a proposal helps you see its exact place in the process:

Before → You have an idea privately. It's still just a thought.

The proposal → You present that idea to others in a structured way and ask for their response.

After → The proposal is either:

  • Accepted → It moves forward and becomes a plan, agreement, law, or commitment.
  • Rejected → It is turned down.
  • Negotiated → It is modified — both parties discuss changes until they reach an agreement.

This is crucial: once a proposal is fully accepted and carried out, it stops being called a proposal. It becomes something else — a deal, a law, a contract, a marriage.
What Makes Something a "Proposal" Rather Than Just an "Idea"?

A private idea in your head is just a thought. It becomes a proposal when you:

  • Present it deliberately to someone else
  • Frame it as something for them to respond to (not just a passing comment)
  • Expect some kind of reaction — an acceptance, a rejection, or a discussion

In other words, a proposal has intent and direction. It is purposeful communication aimed at getting a decision or response from someone.

A proposal can range from very formal to fairly casual:

More formal → A written business proposal with charts, budgets, timelines, and legal language.

Less formal → "I have a proposal — how about we split the work equally?"

In both cases, the word "proposal" fits. What changes is the setting, the stakes, and the structure — not the core meaning.

A proposal is a structured suggestion or offer made by one party to another, with the expectation of a response. It is always forward-looking (suggesting something yet to happen), always directed at someone (never just internal), and always at the "consideration stage" — meaning the outcome is still open and undecided.

Whenever you see or hear the word "proposal," ask yourself two things:

  1. Who is suggesting something?
  2. Who needs to respond to it?

Answer those two questions, and you will always understand what a proposal is in any context.
12904:
When you propose something, you bring an idea, plan, or suggestion forward — you put it in front of others so they can think about it, discuss it, or decide whether to accept or reject it.

The crucial thing to understand: you are not deciding for others. You are offering something for their consideration. A proposal can always be turned down. That possibility is built into the word's very meaning.

1. To suggest a plan, idea, or solution

This is the most common use. You think of something and present it for others to evaluate.

  • "The engineer proposed a new design for the bridge."
  • "She proposed that the team start meetings on Mondays."
  • "He proposed combining both projects into one."

2. To ask someone to marry you

This meaning is so well-known that the word "propose" on its own — with no other words — is universally understood to mean a marriage proposal.

  • "He proposed to her at the top of the Eiffel Tower."
  • "Did you hear? She proposed!" (Everyone immediately understands — she asked someone to marry her.)

You can also say "proposed marriage" if you want to be explicit, but it's rarely necessary.

3. To nominate someone for a position or award

To formally suggest that a specific person should be given a role, title, or recognition.

  • "The committee proposed her for the position of director."
  • "He was proposed as a candidate for the prize."

4. To intend or plan to do something yourself

Here, "propose" doesn't involve others at all — it simply means what you are planning to do. It's a formal way of saying "I plan to" or "I intend to."

  • "What do you propose to do about the water leak?"
  • "The government proposes to reduce income taxes next year."

5. To propose a toast

At a celebration or dinner, when someone raises their glass and invites everyone to drink in honor of something or someone.

  • "I'd like to propose a toast to the happy couple."

Knowing the feel of "propose" is just as important as knowing its definitions.

When you propose something, three things are always true:

  • You are initiating — you are the one bringing the idea into the room.
  • You are inviting — you are opening the door for others to agree, disagree, improve, or reject what you've offered.
  • You are not forcing — a proposal is never an order or a demand.

This is what separates "propose" from words like "decide," "declare," or "demand." Those words close a door. "Propose" opens one.

Propose vs. suggest

Both mean putting an idea forward, but "propose" is more deliberate and formal. You suggest something casually over coffee; you propose something in a meeting, a legal document, or a life-changing moment. That said, people often use them interchangeably in everyday conversation, and that's perfectly natural — "propose" just carries a slightly more serious, considered tone.

Propose vs. recommend

When you recommend something, you personally endorse it — you're saying "I believe this is the best option." When you propose something, you're simply putting it on the table for consideration. A recommendation comes with your approval built in. A proposal doesn't always.

Propose vs. decide

To decide is to reach a final answer. To propose is to begin the conversation toward a possible answer. One is the conclusion; the other is the opening move.

Pattern 1: propose + noun

  • "She proposed a solution."
  • "He proposed an amendment to the law."
  • "They proposed a toast."

Pattern 2: propose + that + subject + verb

  • "I propose that we cancel the meeting."
  • "She proposed that the deadline be extended."

A note on formal writing: After "propose that," the verb often stays in its base form regardless of the subject. So you say "she proposed that he be appointed" — not "he was appointed." This is called the subjunctive mood, and it's common in formal English. In casual speech, people often skip this: "I propose that we start early" is perfectly normal.

Pattern 3: propose + -ing verb

  • "He proposed moving the event to next week."
  • "She proposed splitting the cost equally."

Pattern 4: propose to + person (marriage)

  • "He proposed to her last night."
  • "She proposed to her boyfriend after dinner."

Pattern 5: propose to + base verb (meaning "intend to")

  • "What do you propose to do next?"
  • "The company proposes to expand into three new countries."

"Propose" comfortably crosses formal and informal settings:

  • Formal contexts: board meetings, academic papers, legal documents, parliamentary proceedings ("I propose the motion…"), government announcements.
  • Everyday personal life: marriage proposals, suggesting a plan to friends, proposing a toast at a birthday dinner.

The word doesn't feel out of place in either. Context always makes the meaning clear.

• Proposal (noun) — the thing being proposed. "She made a proposal." "He accepted the proposal."
  • Proposer (noun) — the person who proposes something.
  • Proposed (adjective) — something that has been put forward but not yet decided. "The proposed changes will take effect next year."

To propose is to put forward an idea, plan, or suggestion — formally or personally — so that others (or the situation) can respond to it, with the understanding that what you've offered is open to acceptance, rejection, or discussion.
12905:
A proposition is something that is put forward — an idea, a statement, an offer, or a plan that is placed in front of someone for them to consider, accept, reject, or respond to. Think of it as anything someone "puts on the table."

The word has several distinct meanings depending on the context, and understanding all of them will give you complete command of this word.
Meaning 1: A Statement That Can Be True or False

In logic, philosophy, and academic thinking, a proposition is a clear, definite statement that declares something to be true or false. It is not a question, not a command, not a wish — it is a claim about reality.

  • "The Earth is round" is a proposition. It makes a claim that is either true or false.
  • "All humans are mortal" is a proposition.
  • "Please close the door" is NOT a proposition — it's a command.
  • "Is it raining?" is NOT a proposition — it's a question.

A proposition has to be the kind of statement you can point at and say, "Is this true or false?" If you can do that, it's a proposition.

In mathematics, propositions are statements that can be proven, like: "The sum of two even numbers is always even."

In everyday life and business, a proposition is simply a proposal — an offer or suggestion put forward for someone to consider. This is the most common meaning in ordinary conversation.

  • A company might offer you a business proposition — a deal or plan they want you to agree to.
  • "He came to me with an interesting proposition: I would design the website, and he would handle the marketing."

Here, the proposition is essentially saying: "Here is my offer. What do you think?" It is an invitation to negotiate, agree, or decline.

A value proposition is a popular business term — it means the specific benefit or value a company promises to give its customers. It answers the question: "Why should you choose us?"
Meaning 3: A Task, Situation, or Person Being Considered

In informal usage, "proposition" can describe how difficult, complex, or risky a particular task, situation, or person is. This is used when you want to characterize something in terms of what it demands from you.

  • "Climbing Mount Everest is no easy proposition." → It's a very demanding undertaking.
  • "Dealing with him is a tough proposition." → He is a difficult person to deal with.
  • "Starting a business in this economy is a risky proposition." → It involves considerable risk.

Think of it as saying: "When you consider what this involves, here's what kind of thing it is."
Meaning 4: A Ballot Measure (Politics/Law, especially in the US)

In American politics, a proposition is a specific question or measure put to the public to vote on, usually appearing on a ballot by number.

  • "Proposition 13 changed how property taxes were calculated in California."

Here, a proposition is literally something "put forward" to the voters — they decide whether to approve or reject it.

In informal usage, to receive a proposition can also mean to receive an unsolicited or forward romantic or sexual offer from someone. While this meaning is less formal, it is well-established in everyday language.

  • "She was propositioned by a stranger at the bar." (Here it's used as a verb, but the noun form works the same way: "She received an unwanted proposition.")

Even though these meanings seem different on the surface, they all share the same underlying idea: something is placed in front of you and you must engage with it — by believing it or not, accepting it or not, voting on it or not, or dealing with it.

ContextWhat's being "put forward"
  • In logic → a statement put forward to be judged as true or false
  • In business/life → an offer put forward to be accepted or rejected
  • In everyday speech → a situation or task put forward as something to be dealt with
  • In politics → a measure put forward to be voted on
  • In informal social life → an advance put forward to be welcomed or refused

"A tough proposition" — something or someone that is hard to handle or deal with.

"A risky proposition" — something that involves significant risk.

"A business proposition" — a formal offer or deal in a commercial context.

"A value proposition" — the promise of benefit a product or service makes to a customer.

"An attractive proposition" — something that seems appealing and worth considering.

"Prove a proposition" — to demonstrate logically or mathematically that a statement is true.
The Subtle Difference Between "Proposition" and Similar Words

• A proposition is broader and more formal than a suggestion — it implies something more structured, more serious, or more defined.
  • A proposition is not quite the same as a question — a question asks; a proposition declares or offers.
  • A proposition differs from a fact — a fact is already accepted as true; a proposition is something still being put forward for consideration.

If you ever forget what "proposition" means, remember this simple phrase:

"Something put on the table for you to deal with."

Whether it's a logical statement, a business deal, a ballot measure, or a challenge — all meanings of proposition come back to that single image: something placed before you, waiting for your response.
12906:
To propound something means to put forward an idea, theory, question, or belief for others to consider, examine, or discuss.

Think of it as formally presenting something to the world and saying, "Here — think about this." You're not just casually mentioning it. You're laying it out seriously, with the expectation that people will engage with it, debate it, or at least take notice of it.

The simplest plain-English substitute is: "to put forward" or "to present for consideration."

You don't propound just anything. The word typically attaches to things of intellectual or serious substance:

  • A theory — A scientist propounds a new theory about black holes.
  • A hypothesis — She propounded a hypothesis that the committee debated for hours.
  • A question — He propounded a question so difficult that no one in the room could answer it.
  • A philosophy or doctrine — The thinker propounded a philosophy of radical simplicity.
  • A view or argument — The lawyer propounded his argument before the court.
  • A riddle or puzzle — The teacher propounded a riddle to challenge her students.
The Subtle Flavour of the Word

This is where understanding a word truly deepens. "Propound" carries a few subtle qualities that make it distinct:

1. It implies seriousness and deliberateness.
When someone propounds something, they are doing it with purpose and weight. It's not a throwaway remark. There is an air of intellectual intent behind the act.

2. It does not mean you are proving something.
You are simply presenting it. The idea is being offered up — its truth or validity is still open. A philosopher can propound a theory that turns out to be completely wrong. The word says nothing about whether the idea is right or wrong, only that it is being formally presented.

3. It does not mean you are explaining something in detail.
This is a common mix-up. The word expound means to explain or elaborate on something at length. Propound is about the act of putting the idea forward in the first place — not the act of unpacking it in detail. You propound a theory; you expound upon it.

4. It carries a formal register.
"Propound" is not a word you'd use in everyday casual conversation. You wouldn't say "I propounded to my friend that we should get pizza." It belongs to academic, philosophical, legal, and literary contexts. In everyday speech, people simply say "suggest," "raise," or "put forward."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Since learners often confuse closely related words, here's a clear breakdown:

Propound vs. Suggest
"Suggest" is casual and everyday. "Propound" is formal and carries intellectual weight. You suggest a restaurant; you propound a theory.

Propound vs. Propose
"Propose" often implies seeking a decision, agreement, or action — "I propose we vote on this." "Propound" is more about presenting something for intellectual consideration, not necessarily calling for a vote or a decision.

Propound vs. Posit
"Posit" means to assume something as a starting point or a given, often for the sake of an argument — "Let's posit that X is true." "Propound" is about presenting an idea to the broader world for consideration, not just assuming it momentarily.

Propound vs. Expound
As noted above — to expound is to explain something thoroughly and in detail. To propound is to put something forward for consideration. These two are frequently confused. Remember: propound = present it; expound = explain it.

Propound vs. Advocate
To advocate is to actively and passionately support something. When you propound an idea, you may or may not personally believe it — you are simply presenting it. An academic can propound a theory without personally endorsing it.

• Darwin propounded the theory of natural selection, which changed the course of science forever.
  • During the lecture, the professor propounded several challenging questions that no one could immediately answer.
  • The philosopher propounded a view of morality that was based entirely on reason, not emotion.
  • In court, the attorney propounded a bold new argument in defence of his client.
  • She propounded her ideas about urban design at the international conference.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By

To propound = to put forward a serious idea, theory, or question so that others may consider or debate it.

If you can remember that image — someone standing up, presenting a weighty idea to a room full of people who are now going to think it over — you have captured the word perfectly.
12907:
Proprietary means belonging to, or controlled by, a specific owner — and because of that ownership, others cannot freely use, copy, share, or access it without permission.

Think of it this way: if something is proprietary, someone owns it in a special, protected way, and that ownership gives them the exclusive right to decide who gets to use it, how, and at what price.

The word describes something that:

  1. Is owned by a specific person, company, or organization.
  2. Is not open or free — it's controlled, guarded, or exclusive.
  3. Cannot be freely copied or used by others, usually because the law protects the owner's rights over it.

1. Proprietary Technology or Software

This is where you'll encounter the word most often. When a tech company builds a product — say, a piece of software — and does not allow the public to see how it works inside, or copy it, or build on top of it, that software is called proprietary.

For example, Microsoft Word and Adobe Photoshop are proprietary software. The company owns the code, keeps it secret, and sells you a licence to use it — you don't truly "own" a copy in the full sense; you're paying for permission.

The opposite of proprietary software is open-source software, where the inner workings are shared publicly and anyone can inspect, use, or modify it. So whenever you see "proprietary" in the tech world, think: closed, owned, and controlled by one company.

2. Proprietary Information or Data

Companies often have sensitive knowledge — a secret recipe, a unique manufacturing process, a customer database, a business strategy. This is called proprietary information (also known as a trade secret).

Calling it proprietary signals that it belongs to the company, it is not to be shared outside, and sharing it without permission could be illegal. Think of KFC's original fried chicken recipe — that's proprietary. Nobody outside the company is supposed to know the exact formula.

3. Proprietary Products

When a company manufactures and sells a product under its own brand name, and others aren't allowed to make or sell the same thing, that product is described as proprietary.

A real-world example: brand-name medicines. When a drug company invents a new medicine, they receive a patent (legal protection of ownership) and only they can make and sell it for a number of years. During that period, it is a proprietary drug. Once the patent expires, other companies can make the same medicine under a different (generic) name — and it's no longer proprietary.

4. A Proprietary System or Format

Sometimes companies design systems, tools, or file formats that only work with their own products. You can't use them with a competitor's product, and you can't independently build something compatible without the company's permission.

For example, imagine a brand of coffee machine that only works with that brand's coffee pods — no other pods fit. The pod design is proprietary. This is sometimes called vendor lock-in, because once you buy into the system, you depend on that one company entirely.
What Makes Something "Proprietary"? (The Legal Angle, Simplified)

Ownership of a physical thing — like a chair — is easy to understand. But proprietary things are usually ideas, inventions, designs, or information, which are harder to "own." That's why laws exist to protect them. These are called Intellectual Property (IP) rights, and they come in different forms:

  • Patents protect inventions and new technologies.
  • Trademarks protect brand names and logos.
  • Copyrights protect creative works like writing, music, and software.
  • Trade secrets protect confidential business information.

When something is proprietary, it usually means one or more of these legal protections are in place, giving the owner the exclusive right to control it.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Proprietary" often carries a sense of exclusivity and restriction. It quietly communicates: "This is ours. You don't have free access to this."

Depending on context, this can be:

  • Neutral — just a factual statement of ownership. ("This is our proprietary blend of spices.")
  • Positive — suggesting something special, unique, or premium. ("Our proprietary formula is more effective than anything else on the market.")
  • Negative or suspicious — implying secrecy, control, or an attempt to trap customers. ("The company uses a proprietary format so you can't move your data to a competitor.")
A Common Trap: Don't Confuse "Proprietary" with Just "Private"

Something private simply means it isn't shared openly. Something proprietary goes a step further — it is legally owned, and that ownership is the reason it isn't shared. The legal protection is the key difference.

A person's diary is private. A company's patented drug formula is proprietary.

ConceptWhat it means simply
ProprietaryOwned by a specific person or company, with legal rights to control its use
Proprietary softwareSoftware whose code is owned and kept secret by a company
Proprietary informationSecret business knowledge belonging to a company
Proprietary productA product exclusively made/sold under one company's ownership
Opposite of proprietaryOpen, public domain, open-source, generic
One Sentence to Remember It By

Proprietary = owned exclusively, with the legal right to control who uses it and how.

Every time you see this word, ask yourself: who owns this, and what are they restricting because of that ownership? The answer will always reveal what "proprietary" means in that specific context.
12908: A proprietor is a person who owns something — most commonly a business, a shop, or a piece of property. Ownership is the single most important idea packed into this word.

When someone is called a proprietor, it means three things are almost always true:

1. They own it. The business or property legally belongs to them. They didn't just get hired to work there — it is theirs.

2. They control it. Because they own it, they get to make the big decisions. They decide the prices, the rules, the hours, and the direction of the business. Nobody above them is giving orders.

3. They are responsible for it. If the business succeeds, the reward is theirs. If it fails or causes problems, the responsibility falls on them too. Ownership comes with both the power and the weight.

Think of it this way: a proprietor is not just in a business — they are the business.
Who Gets Called a Proprietor in Real Life?

The word is most naturally used for people who own and personally run smaller or independent businesses. For example:

  • The person who owns and runs a small hotel or inn.
  • The person who owns a local bookshop or hardware store.
  • The person who owns a restaurant and is often seen managing it themselves.
  • A person who owns a piece of land or real estate.

You would be less likely to call the CEO of a massive corporation like Apple a "proprietor," because large corporations are owned by thousands of shareholders, not a single person. The word works best when one person (or a small group) has clear, direct ownership.

You will very commonly hear the phrase sole proprietor. "Sole" simply means one or only. So a sole proprietor is someone who owns an entire business completely on their own — no business partners, no co-owners, no shareholders splitting ownership with them.

It is the simplest and most common form of business ownership in the world. A freelance photographer, a self-employed plumber, or a person running a small home bakery are all examples of sole proprietors — they own and operate their business single-handedly.
Proprietor vs. Words That Sound Similar

Understanding a word deeply means knowing how it is different from nearby words.

Proprietor vs. Manager
A manager runs a business but does not own it. They answer to someone above them. A proprietor is the person at the top — they own it. A proprietor can also be their own manager, but a manager is never automatically a proprietor.

Proprietor vs. Employee
An employee works for someone in exchange for wages. A proprietor is the person the employee works for.

Proprietor vs. Partner
Partners co-own a business together. Each partner can be called a proprietor in a general sense, but when ownership is shared equally between partners, they are more specifically called co-owners or partners rather than sole proprietors.

Proprietor vs. Landlord
A landlord is actually a type of proprietor — someone who owns property and rents it to others. But "proprietor" is the broader word. All landlords are proprietors of their property, but not all proprietors are landlords.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Proprietor" is a slightly formal word. It carries a sense of dignity, authority, and pride of ownership. You are more likely to see it on a sign outside an old-fashioned shop, in a legal document, or in formal writing than in casual everyday conversation.

In casual speech, people usually just say "owner." But "proprietor" means essentially the same thing — it just sounds more official and traditional. For example, an antique shop might display a sign reading: "J. Harrison, Proprietor, Est. 1948."

• Proprietors — the plural. "The two proprietors agreed to merge their businesses."
  • Proprietorship — the noun referring to the state of being a proprietor, or the business itself. "She built a successful sole proprietorship over twenty years."
  • Proprietary — the adjective form, meaning "relating to an owner or ownership," or something exclusively owned and controlled by one party. "This is proprietary software" means the software is exclusively owned and controlled by one company.
  • Proprietress — a now rarely used, old-fashioned feminine form meaning a female proprietor. Modern usage simply says "proprietor" for all genders.

• "The proprietor of the café personally greeted every customer who walked through the door."
  • "As the sole proprietor of his accounting firm, he was responsible for every decision, big or small."
  • "The new proprietor renovated the entire hotel before reopening it to guests."
  • "She had always dreamed of becoming the proprietor of her own flower shop."
  • "The landlord, who was also the proprietor of several buildings downtown, raised the rents."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: a proprietor is an owner — especially of a business or property — someone who holds the rights, the control, and the responsibility that come with that ownership.
12909:
Propriety means correct and appropriate behavior — the kind of behavior that a society, a group, or a particular situation considers proper, fitting, and acceptable. It is about doing and saying the right thing, in the right place, in the right way, at the right time — not purely by your own private judgment, but according to the shared standards of those around you.

Think of it this way: every situation in life comes with invisible rules. At a funeral, you dress somberly and speak quietly. In a formal business meeting, you avoid crude jokes. When meeting someone's elderly grandmother for the first time, you don't use slang. When you follow these unwritten rules naturally and correctly, you are behaving with propriety.
Propriety is not the same as morality

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. Propriety is not about being a good person in a moral or ethical sense. A person can be deeply kind and honest on the inside, and still lack propriety — perhaps they speak too bluntly at a dinner party, share a personal story that makes everyone uncomfortable, or show up to a formal event in casual clothes.

Propriety is about the surface of social life — manners, appearance, speech, and conduct as judged by others in a given situation. It is the art of fitting smoothly into the social expectations of a moment. Conversely, someone can have impeccable propriety and still be a deeply selfish or dishonest person. The two things are separate.

This is what makes the word interesting and slightly tricky: propriety's standards are not fixed or universal. They shift depending on the culture you are in, the time period you are living in, and the specific situation you find yourself in.

What is considered proper in one country may seem strange or even rude in another. Victorian-era propriety was extremely strict — rigid rules about women's dress, formal introductions before speaking to a stranger, never discussing money in polite company — rules we now find laughably stiff. And what is proper at a beach party is very different from what is proper at a court of law.

So propriety is always defined relative to a context. What the word always means, no matter the context, is this: behaving according to the accepted norms of wherever and whenever you are.

When the word is used in the plural — the proprieties — it refers to the specific rules or customs of proper behavior in a given setting, thought of one by one.

For example: "She always observed the proprieties at formal dinners." This means she followed each of the specific rules of formal dining — the right fork, the right posture, the right topics of conversation. "He ignored the proprieties of the occasion" means he broke the accepted social rules of that particular event.

A useful way to think about it: propriety (singular) is the overall quality of behaving correctly, while the proprieties (plural) are the individual items on the checklist of correct behavior.

A sense of propriety refers to an inner awareness of what is socially appropriate. Someone with a strong sense of propriety naturally knows what to do and say in various situations without being told — it is almost instinctive to them.

To behave with propriety means to conduct oneself in a proper, fitting manner. "She handled the difficult question with propriety" means she dealt with it in exactly the right, socially acceptable way.

A breach of propriety (sometimes called a violation of propriety) means breaking the rules of acceptable social behavior. This is usually something that causes embarrassment or offense, though not necessarily something illegal or deeply immoral. A crude joke at a funeral is a breach of propriety. So is a politician using an official visit for personal gain.

To observe the proprieties means to follow the accepted rules of polite or formal behavior in full. It suggests deliberate, careful attention to doing everything correctly.

Questions of propriety are situations where people debate whether something is appropriate or not — for instance, whether it is proper for a judge to publicly comment on a case they are handling.
The tone and feel of the word

Propriety has a formal, slightly old-fashioned quality to it. You would not hear it casually in everyday conversation. You are far more likely to encounter it in formal writing, literary fiction, discussions of etiquette, historical contexts (it was a very important concept in the 18th and 19th centuries), and professional or institutional settings.

When someone lacks propriety, or when a specific action is socially inappropriate, the word for that is impropriety — the direct opposite of propriety.

A few scenarios that show the full range of propriety:

At a funeral, a person who cracks loud jokes, takes selfies, and laughs boisterously is behaving without propriety. Someone who dresses somberly, speaks gently, and focuses on comforting the grieving family is showing propriety.

At a board meeting, an employee who interrupts senior colleagues, uses slang, and checks their phone repeatedly is violating propriety. An employee who listens attentively, speaks formally when addressed, and waits their turn demonstrates propriety.

In a letter of condolence, writing something dismissive like "Well, these things happen — life goes on!" would be a breach of propriety. A warm, careful, and respectful letter shows propriety in written communication.

A journalist who secretly records a private conversation for a story might be technically breaking no law, but many would argue it is still a breach of professional propriety.
One final sentence to lock it in

Propriety is the quality of behaving in a way that is considered correct, fitting, and socially acceptable for a particular situation — not by your own private standards alone, but according to the shared expectations of the people and culture around you.
